units.title: Unit 41 — Sport and leisure
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 88–89 (PDF pages 89–90).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition)
learningObjectives: Identify the names of major sports, participants, playing areas and equipment.
Use play, go and do with the appropriate sports or leisure activities.
Describe camping, jogging, rock climbing, yoga and exercise routines.
Use work out, keep fit, for fun and for pleasure in natural contexts.
Recognise sport-person word families and classify sports vocabulary by use.

items.example: My sister practises athletics after school.
items.note: A sport including running, jumping and throwing events.

items.example: The young athlete trains every morning.
items.note: A person who competes in athletics or other sports.

items.example: Motor racing attracts thousands of spectators.
items.note: A sport in which people race motor vehicles.

items.example: The racing driver wore a protective helmet.
items.note: Someone who drives a vehicle in motor races.

items.example: Swimming is good exercise for many people.
items.note: A sport or activity done in water.

items.example: The swimmer reached the other side of the pool.
items.note: Someone who swims.

items.example: Boxing requires balance and quick movements.
items.note: A sport in which two people fight using their fists.

items.example: The boxer trained before the next match.
items.note: Someone who takes part in boxing.

items.example: Skiing is popular in the mountains in winter.
items.note: Moving over snow on skis.

items.example: The skier moved carefully down the mountain.
items.note: Someone who skis.

items.example: Football is played in many countries.
items.note: British English: the sport called soccer in American English.

items.pt: jogador de futebol; jogadora de futebol
items.example: The footballer scored just before half-time.
items.note: Someone who plays football, especially professionally.

items.example: Ice hockey players move quickly across the ice.
items.note: A team sport played on ice using sticks and a puck.

items.pt: jogador de hóquei no gelo; jogadora de hóquei no gelo
items.example: Each ice hockey player wore a helmet.
items.note: A person who plays ice hockey.

items.example: My aunt plays golf on Sundays.
items.note: A sport played by hitting a small ball into a series of holes.

items.example: The golfer practised putting before the match.
items.note: Someone who plays golf.

items.example: Basketball is my favourite team sport.
items.note: A game in which teams try to throw a ball through a basket.

items.pt: jogador de basquete; jogadora de basquete
items.example: The basketball player passed the ball to a teammate.
items.note: A person who plays basketball.

items.example: Sailing is easier when the weather is calm.
items.note: A sport or activity involving boats moved by the wind.

items.example: The sailor checked the wind before leaving.
items.note: In this unit, someone who sails a boat for sport.

items.example: The goalkeeper caught the ball near the goal.
items.note: A player who tries to prevent the other team from scoring.

items.example: The ball hit the net behind the goalkeeper.
items.note: Sports equipment made of connected threads or cords.

items.example: We put our skis in the car before leaving.
items.note: Plural of ski; long, narrow equipment for travelling over snow.

items.example: The ice hockey player lifted the stick.
items.note: A long piece of equipment used to move the puck in hockey.

items.example: She packed her swimming costume for the pool.
items.note: British English: clothing worn for swimming.

items.pt: pista de atletismo; pista de corrida
items.example: The runners warmed up on the track.
items.note: An area where races are held, often inside a stadium.

items.example: The stadium was full for the final.
items.note: A large sports venue with seats for spectators.

items.example: The children were learning to swim in the pool.
items.note: A place where people swim.

items.example: Both boxers stepped into the boxing ring.
items.note: The enclosed area where a boxing match takes place.

items.example: The ski slopes opened after heavy snow.
items.note: Snowy hills prepared or used for skiing.

items.example: The players ran onto the football pitch.
items.note: British English: the playing area for football and some other sports.

items.example: They practised on the ice hockey rink before lunch.
items.note: The ice surface used for ice hockey.

items.example: There is a golf course near the lake.
items.note: The outdoor area designed for playing golf.

items.example: Our school has a new basketball court.
items.note: A marked playing area for basketball.

items.example: I run in the park before work.
items.note: Athletes run in races; past tense: ran.

items.example: You have to jump over the bar in this event.
items.note: An action used in some athletics events.

items.example: Can you swim all the way across the pool?
items.note: The verb linked to swimming; swim, swam, swum.

items.example: The athlete tried to throw the ball further.
items.note: An action used in some athletics events; past tense: threw.

items.example: Several young people will race tomorrow.
items.note: Verb: try to be the fastest in a race.

items.example: He began to box when he was a teenager.
items.note: Verb: take part in boxing.

items.example: The two boxers will fight next weekend.
items.note: Verb used in boxing; fight, fought, fought.

items.example: Can you ski on steep slopes?
items.note: Verb related to skiing; also a noun for the equipment.

items.example: We plan to sail across the lake.
items.note: Verb: travel on water using a boat, often with sails.

items.example: We play football every Friday afternoon.
items.note: Use play with team and ball sports, including football.

items.example: My classmates play basketball after school.
items.note: Use play with basketball, tennis, golf and similar sports.

items.example: We go swimming at the leisure centre.
items.note: Go commonly combines with activities ending in -ing.

items.example: I sometimes go rock climbing with friends.
items.note: Use go with this -ing activity; it requires suitable equipment and training.

items.example: We did a bit of sailing during our holiday.
items.note: Do a bit of + -ing describes a small amount of an activity.

items.example: She does a lot of running before races.
items.note: Do a lot of + -ing describes frequent or extensive activity.

items.example: Our tent kept us dry during the rain.
items.note: Portable shelter used when camping.

items.example: Camping is popular in this national park.
items.note: Staying outdoors, usually in a tent.

items.example: We might go camping by the river in July.
items.note: A common go + -ing collocation.

items.example: Rock climbing requires strength and care.
items.note: Climbing natural or artificial rock surfaces.

items.example: Jogging helps him relax after a busy day.
items.note: Running slowly for exercise.

items.pt: sair para correr; fazer corrida leve
items.example: My neighbour likes to go jogging at sunrise.
items.note: A common go + -ing expression.

items.example: Yoga can improve flexibility with regular practice.
items.note: An activity combining physical positions, breathing and concentration.

items.example: He does yoga at home every evening.
items.note: Use do, not play, with yoga.

items.example: The gym closes at nine in the evening.
items.note: A place with equipment for physical exercise.

items.example: I go to the gym twice a week.
items.note: A common expression for visiting a place to exercise.

items.example: They work out together after work.
items.note: Phrasal verb: exercise, especially at a gym.

items.pt: manter a forma; manter o condicionamento físico
items.example: Cycling to work helps me keep fit.
items.note: Stay in good physical condition.

items.example: We play tennis for fun, not to win prizes.
items.note: Means for enjoyment, not necessarily for a serious purpose.

items.example: She swims for pleasure at weekends.
items.note: A close alternative to for fun.

items.example: Regular exercise can improve your health.
items.note: As a noun referring to physical activity, it is often uncountable.

items.example: I try to do exercise before breakfast.
items.note: A natural collocation for physical activity; not play exercise.

items.example: Our club offers leisure activities for adults.
items.note: Things people do in their free time.

units.title: Unit 42 — Competitive sport
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 90–91 (PDF pages 91–92).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition)
learningObjectives: Report victories, defeats, draws and scores using the correct verb patterns.
Distinguish final results from the score at half-time and read scores aloud.
Describe individuals, teams, tournaments, leagues, cups and finals.
Use win/won/won, lose/lost/lost, beat/beat/beaten, draw/drew/drawn and break/broke/broken.
Understand sports reporting language including records, victories, medals and evaluative adjectives.

items.example: Do you know the score in the football match?
items.note: The number of goals or points each side has.

items.example: Our team hopes to win the final.
items.note: Use win with a game, match, prize or competition; win, won, won.

items.example: They may lose if they do not defend well.
items.note: Irregular verb: lose, lost, lost.

items.pt: vencer uma equipe; derrotar um time
items.example: Their team managed to beat a stronger team.
items.note: Beat takes an opponent as its object: beat them, not win them; beat, beat, beaten.

items.example: Our school managed to defeat a local team.
items.note: Defeat takes the defeated opponent as its object; often more formal than beat.

items.example: We did not expect to lose to a new team.
items.note: Pattern: lose to + opponent; past: lost to.

items.example: The teams are likely to draw on Saturday.
items.note: Verb meaning finish with the same score; draw, drew, drawn.

items.example: The match ended in a draw.
items.note: Noun: a match where neither team wins.

items.example: Our team drew with the visitors yesterday.
items.note: Pattern: draw with + opponent; draw, drew, drawn.

items.example: The home side were still on nil after an hour.
items.note: Used for zero when giving a score, especially in British football.

items.example: At the break, the score was two nil.
items.note: Spoken form of a 2–0 sports score; it gives no team names by itself.

items.example: The game finished one all after an exciting second half.
items.note: Spoken form of a 1–1 draw in football.

items.example: We waited to hear the result of the match.
items.note: In this sense, the result is the final outcome, not the half-time score.

items.example: The final score was three goals to one.
items.note: The score when a game has finished.

items.example: The final result surprised both coaches.
items.note: The outcome after the match ends.

items.example: They changed their plan at half-time.
items.note: The break between the two halves of a match.

items.example: The score at half-time was one all.
items.note: Say score at half-time, not result at half-time.

items.example: The competition begins next month at the local stadium.
items.note: An organised event in which people try to win.

items.example: Each individual receives a race number.
items.note: Here, a single competitor rather than a team.

items.example: The whole team practised together before the match.
items.note: A group of people who play or compete together.

items.example: Children can take part in the local tournament.
items.note: Followed by an event or activity; past: took part in.

items.pt: inscrever-se em um torneio; participar de um torneio
items.example: She hopes to enter a tournament in May.
items.note: Enter means register or compete in an organised tournament.

items.example: The tennis tournament lasts a week.
items.note: A series of matches or contests to decide the winner.

items.example: The team joined a regional league.
items.note: A competition in which teams regularly play one another.

items.pt: competição de liga; campeonato de pontos corridos
items.example: The club plays in a league competition each season.
items.note: Teams play against other teams in the league; not the same format as a knockout cup.

items.example: Our team will play against the visitors on Sunday.
items.note: Against introduces the opposing player or team.

items.example: The club reached the last round of the cup competition.
items.note: A competition that may involve knockout rounds leading to a final.

items.example: The captain lifted the cup after the final.
items.note: Here, a trophy awarded to winners of a sports competition.

items.example: Thousands of fans watched the final.
items.note: The last match or event deciding the winner.

items.example: The winner received a silver trophy.
items.note: Someone who wins an event or competition.

items.example: The loser congratulated the winner after the match.
items.note: In sport, the player or team that loses; opposite of winner.

items.example: The champion returned to defend her title.
items.note: A competitor or team that wins a major competition.

items.example: The captain spoke to the team before the match.
items.note: The player who leads a sports team.

items.example: The swimmer set a new world record.
items.note: The best officially recorded performance anywhere in the world.

items.pt: quebrar um recorde; superar uma marca
items.example: She hopes to break a record at the next meeting.
items.note: Achieve a better result than the previous record; break, broke, broken.

items.example: The fans celebrated an unexpected victory.
items.note: A success in a game, race or competition; opposite: defeat.

items.example: The club suffered a heavy defeat last night.
items.note: As a noun, defeat is the opposite of victory; it can also be a verb.

items.example: The team achieved an important victory away from home.
items.note: Formal reporting collocation: achieve a victory.

items.example: She won the national championship last year.
items.note: A major competition or the title gained by winning it.

items.example: He gave up competitive cycling after an injury.
items.note: Phrasal verb: stop doing an activity; give up, gave up, given up. Often followed by -ing.

items.example: The visitors lead by two points.
items.note: Present: lead; past and participle: led.

items.example: The race finished later than expected.
items.note: A competition to see who can travel a distance fastest.

items.example: The athlete won a gold medal at the games.
items.note: An award for first place in many sporting events.

items.example: She won three consecutive races in one month.
items.note: Describes events that happen one after another without a break.

items.example: That was an incredible performance under pressure.
items.note: A very strong positive adjective for something remarkable.

items.example: The goalkeeper gave an outstanding performance.
items.note: Means exceptionally good; common in sports reports.

items.example: The young player showed superb control.
items.note: A strong adjective meaning very high quality.

items.example: The team reached the semi-final on Tuesday.
items.note: A round in which the winners progress to the final.

items.example: Maya hopes to come first in the swimming race.
items.note: To finish in first place; irregular past: came first.

items.example: Our school came second in the competition.
items.note: To finish in second place.

items.example: I came third in the short-distance race.
items.note: To finish in third place.
